body:
## Problem

`computeIntersection` builds the conjunction of N ranges by string-joining them (`intersect.ts:96` `combined = ${combined} ${entry.range}`, and `intersect.ts:112` `simplified.join(' ')`). In semver grammar `||` binds looser than the space (AND) operator, so joining `A || B` with `C` yields `A || (B C)`, not `(A || B) && C`. Any input range containing `||` produces a semantically wrong result — the tool's single headline output.

## Evidence

Ran against the real implementation:

    computeIntersection([{range: '^17 || ^18'}, {range: '^16 || ^18'}])
    -> ">=16.0.0 <17.0.0-0 || >=18.0.0 <18.0.0-0 || >=18.0.0 <19.0.0-0"
       16.5.0: reported=true  truth=false   <<< WRONG

    computeIntersection([{range: '^14 || ^16 || ^18'}, {range: '^16 || ^18 || ^20'}])
    -> ">=14.0.0 <15.0.0-0 || >=16.0.0 <17.0.0-0 || >=18.0.0 <17.0.0-0 || ..."
       14.1.0: reported=true truth=false   <<< WRONG
       20.1.0: reported=true truth=false   <<< WRONG

The emitted string even contains the unsatisfiable group `>=18.0.0 <17.0.0-0`, proving the reconstruction is malformed rather than merely imprecise.

## Impact

`^18 || ^19` style peer ranges are the norm for react/vue/webpack, and `^18 || ^20 || ^22` is the norm for `engines.node`. For any such input the tool reports node/peer versions as safe that satisfy only one input constraint. A user who pins CI to a version the tool blessed gets a broken install. This is the product's core claim.

## Fix

Never concatenate range strings. Build the conjunction with semver's own range algebra, distributing the AND over each OR-set:

    import semver from 'semver'
    function andRanges(a: string, b: string): string | null {
      const out: string[] = []
      for (const ga of new semver.Range(a).set)
        for (const gb of new semver.Range(b).set) {
          const g = [...ga, ...gb].map(c => c.value).filter(v => v !== '').join(' ') || '*'
          if (semver.validRange(g) !== null && semver.subset(g, g)) out.push(g)
        }
      const joined = out.join(' || ')
      return semver.validRange(joined)
    }

then fold with `andRanges` instead of template-string concatenation, and drop OR-groups that are empty (`semver.minVersion(group) === null`). Feed the per-group result through `simplifyComparators` (which already operates per-group and is correct) before joining with `||`. Regression test: assert `semver.satisfies(v, result) === (satisfies(v, r1) && satisfies(v, r2))` for every `v` in a sampled set, over inputs containing `||`.

## Resolution
Replaced string-concatenation with andRanges() in src/analyzer/intersect.ts: the AND is distributed across both OR-sets and groups whose semver.minVersion() is null (unsatisfiable) are dropped. filterSubsumed deleted - the fold now produces the tightest result directly. Verified: ['^17 || ^18','^16 || ^18'] now yields '>=18.0.0 <19.0.0-0' (was admitting 16.5.0). 9 new semantic tests in test/analyzer/intersect.test.ts assert satisfies(v,result) === every(satisfies(v,input)) over a 10-version sample, plus a test that no unsatisfiable OR-group is ever emitted.
title: OR-ranges corrupted by string concatenation; wrong safe range reported

body:
## Problem

`resolveLocal` looks up `node_modules/<name>/package.json` by name only (`local.ts:18`, `local.ts:34`) and applies the result to every `Package` with that name. A lockfile legitimately contains several versions of the same package; node_modules holds exactly one hoisted copy. Every non-hoisted version gets the hoisted version's `engines` and `peerDependencies`.

## Evidence

Ran the real function against a temp project whose node_modules holds `foo@3.0.0` with `engines.node: ">=20"`:

    resolveLocal([{name:'foo',version:'3.0.0'}, {name:'foo',version:'1.0.0'}], dir)
    -> [{"name":"foo","version":"3.0.0","engines":{"node":">=20"}},
        {"name":"foo","version":"1.0.0","engines":{"node":">=20"}}]

`foo@1.0.0` is reported as requiring node >=20 purely because 3.0.0 is hoisted. Pass 1 runs before the registry pass, and `client.ts:122` only overwrites when the registry lookup succeeds — so with `--offline`, or on any registry miss, the fabricated constraint survives into the final intersection.

## Impact

Fabricated constraints narrow (or, symmetrically, widen) the computed safe range. In `--offline` mode, which the README advertises as a first-class mode, this is the only data source, so the wrong answer is the only answer.

## Fix

Verify the manifest's version before using it, in `readLocalManifest`'s caller:

    const manifest = readLocalManifest(pkg.name, projectDir)
    if (manifest === null || manifest.version !== pkg.version) return pkg

and add `version?: string` to the `PackageManifest` interface (local.ts:5). Optionally fall back to the nested copy at `node_modules/<parent>/node_modules/<name>/package.json` before giving up. Test: two entries of one name, one version present in node_modules — assert the other keeps `engines === undefined`.

## Resolution
src/registry/local.ts now skips the manifest when manifest.version is a string and differs from pkg.version; added version?: string to PackageManifest. A manifest with no version field still applies (unchanged behaviour). Two tests in test/registry/local.test.ts cover both paths.
title: resolveLocal stamps the hoisted manifest onto every version of a package

body:
## Problem

For pnpm v9 the parser iterates `snapshots` for the package list but looks the metadata up in `packages` using the _unstripped_ snapshot key (`pnpm.ts:65` `const meta = metaBlock[key] ?? {}`). In the v9 format `snapshots` keys carry a peer-resolution suffix — `vue-router@4.2.5(vue@3.3.4)` — while `packages` keys never do. The lookup misses and `meta` falls back to `{}`. `extractNameVersion` already strips the suffix at `pnpm.ts:26`; the metadata lookup does not.

## Evidence

Ran the real parser on a minimal v9 lockfile where `packages` declares `engines: { node: '>=18' }` and `peerDependencies: { vue: ^3.2.0 }` for `vue-router@4.2.5`, and `snapshots` keys it as `vue-router@4.2.5(vue@3.3.4)`:

    parsePnpmLockfile(yaml)
    -> [{"name":"vue-router","version":"4.2.5"}]      // engines/peerDependencies gone

The committed fixture `test/fixtures/pnpm-lock-v9.yaml` has no peer-suffixed snapshot keys, so the whole test suite passes over this path.

## Impact

Every peer-dependent package in a real pnpm v9 lockfile — which is exactly the population whose `peerDependencies` this tool exists to analyze — contributes no constraints. With `--offline` nothing recovers them and the reported safe range is silently too permissive.

## Fix

Strip the suffix before the metadata lookup:

    const stripped = key.replace(/\([^)]*\)/gu, '').trim()
    const meta = metaBlock[stripped] ?? metaBlock[key] ?? {}

Add a peer suffix to `test/fixtures/pnpm-lock-v9.yaml` (e.g. a `vue-router@4.2.5(vue@3.3.4)` snapshot entry backed by a plain `packages` entry with `engines`) and assert engines survive.

## Resolution
src/parsers/pnpm.ts strips the peer-resolution suffix before the metadata lookup: metaBlock[strippedKey] ?? metaBlock[key] ?? {}. Two tests in test/parsers/pnpm.test.ts use a v9 lockfile whose snapshot key is 'vue-router@4.2.5(vue@3.3.4)' and assert engines and peerDependencies both survive.
title: pnpm v9: engines and peerDependencies dropped for peer-suffixed snapshots

body:
## Problem

Every registry failure path returns `null` and is discarded: `client.ts:58` (`if (!res.ok) return null`), `client.ts:66` (`catch { return null }`), and the same pair at `client.ts:91`/`client.ts:101`. `processBatch` then falls back to whatever was already on the package (`client.ts:122-123`), which for yarn and npm-v1 lockfiles is `undefined`. Nothing counts, reports, or surfaces the failures.

## Impact

Missing constraint data is indistinguishable from "no constraint declared". Because the output is an _intersection_, dropping constraints can only make the reported range wider — the tool fails open in the direction that produces a falsely reassuring answer. A transient DNS failure, a rate limit (npm returns 429 to unauthenticated bulk clients), or an offline corporate proxy all yield a clean-looking table with no warning. The spinner even prints `Fetching registry data... 214/214` on completion, implying success.

## Evidence

Simulate by pointing at an unreachable registry: every fetch throws, every `catch` returns null, and the run still exits 0 with a rendered table. The existing test `fetchManifest: fetch throws → no crash, package returned unchanged` (test/registry/client.test.ts) asserts exactly this silent behaviour as correct.

## Fix

Thread a failure count through `CacheCounter` (rename to a result accumulator), increment it on every `!res.ok` / `catch`, and have `resolveRegistry` return it. In `cli.ts` after the registry pass, when `failed > 0`, write to stderr:

    console.error(`Warning: ${failed}/${packages.length} packages could not be resolved from the registry; the reported ranges may be too permissive.`)

Also render an explicit `unresolved` count in the `--json` payload so CI consumers can gate on it.

## Resolution
CacheCounter gained a 'failed' field, incremented at every !res.ok / !data.version / catch site in fetchManifest and fetchLatest. resolveRegistry now returns { packages, failed } (ResolveResult) and cli.ts prints a stderr warning naming the count and stating the ranges may be too permissive. Three tests cover non-ok, thrown, and offline. Note: writing these tests caught a real miss - fetchLatest's catch had not been given the increment.
title: Registry failures silently widen the reported safe range

body:
## Problem

Three separate paths that should catch a type or lint error all fail to gate:

1. `ci.yml:33` runs `npm run lint`, which is `prettier --write . && eslint --fix .` (package.json:16). It mutates the checkout and then the workflow discards it. Formatting violations and auto-fixable lint errors are silently repaired and never reported.
2. `.mega-linter.yml` `DISABLE_LINTERS` includes `TYPESCRIPT_ES` and `JAVASCRIPT_ES`, so the PR Lint workflow does not lint TS/JS either.
3. There is no `typecheck` script and no `tsc --noEmit` step. The build is `tsup` (package.json:14), which transpiles via esbuild and performs **no** type checking, and `tsconfig.json` sets `"noEmit": true` so `tsc` is never invoked by the build at all.

## Evidence

`grep -n 'tsc' package.json .github/workflows/*.yml` returns nothing. `tsup.config.ts:8` sets `dts: false`, confirming no `tsc` pass in the bundle step. Locally `npx tsc --noEmit` exits 0 today — but nothing in CI would notice if that changed.

## Impact

A type error, or any lint error a human would have to fix, reaches `main` and then npm via `publish.yml`, which runs `npm run build` with no verification gate. The repo is `strict: true` TypeScript whose strictness is never enforced.

## Fix

Add to package.json scripts:

    "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit",
    "lint": "prettier --check . && eslint .",
    "lint:fix": "prettier --write . && eslint --fix ."

and in `ci.yml`, replace the single lint step with:

    - run: npm run lint
    - run: npm run typecheck

Keep `lint:fix` for local use and update the README Development table (README "Development" section) which currently documents `npm run lint` as "Prettier format + ESLint auto-fix".

## Resolution
package.json: 'lint' is now 'prettier --check . && eslint .' (gating), auto-fix moved to 'lint:fix', and a 'typecheck' script runs 'tsc --noEmit'. ci.yml runs lint then typecheck. Verified the new gate works: it immediately failed on an unformatted README during this run. README and CLAUDE.md command tables updated. .mega-linter.yml still disables TYPESCRIPT_ES, which is now correct - ci.yml owns TS linting.
title: No gating lint or typecheck for TypeScript anywhere in CI

body:
## Problem

`buildEdgeMap` derives the node name by stripping only the leading `node_modules/` (`graph/index.ts:44` `key.slice('node_modules/'.length)`). npm v2/v3 lockfiles key non-hoisted packages by their full nested path, so `node_modules/app-dep/node_modules/nested` becomes the node name `app-dep/node_modules/nested`, which no edge list ever references.

## Evidence

Ran the real function on a v3 lockfile with one nested package:

    buildEdgeMap(lock, 'npm')
    -> [ ['app-dep', ['nested']],
         ['app-dep/node_modules/nested', ['deep']],
         ['deep', []] ]

`bfs` (graph/index.ts:107) looks up `'nested'`, finds no entry, and stops. `deep` — reachable in reality only through `nested` — is never visited.

## Impact

`--no-dev` classifies packages by set membership: anything in `devReachable` but not `productionSet` is dropped (graph/index.ts:145-148). A production package reachable only through a non-hoisted intermediate is absent from `productionSet`, so if anything dev-side also reaches it, it is wrongly excluded — and its `engines` constraint vanishes from the intersection, widening the reported safe range.

## Fix

Key by the last path segment, matching `parsers/npm.ts:38-39`:

    const name = key.split('node_modules/').at(-1)
    if (typeof name === 'undefined') continue
    edges.set(name, Object.keys(entry.dependencies ?? {}))

Merge rather than overwrite when the same name appears at several depths, so a nested copy's edges do not clobber the hoisted copy's. Test with the nested lockfile above and assert `deep` is in `bfs(['app-dep'], edges)`.

## Resolution
src/graph/index.ts npm branch keys edges by key.split('node_modules/').at(-1), matching parsers/npm.ts, and unions dependency lists when a name appears both hoisted and nested rather than clobbering. Two tests assert edges.get('nested') === ['deep'] and that the union case yields ['a','b'].
title: npm v2/v3 edge map keys nested packages by path, breaking --no-dev
--no-dev silently degrades to direct-dependencies-only on yarn berry

body:
## Problem

`parseYarnBerryLockfile` returns only `{ name, version }` (`yarn-berry.ts:29`) and types the parse result as `Record<string, Record<string, string>>` (`yarn-berry.ts:10`), which structurally cannot hold the nested `peerDependencies` / `dependencies` maps that Yarn Berry lockfiles do contain for every resolution.

## Evidence

A Yarn Berry `yarn.lock` entry looks like:

    "react-dom@npm:18.3.1":
      version: 18.3.1
      peerDependencies:
        react: ^18.3.1

`parseSyml` returns that nested map, and the parser drops it. The npm and pnpm parsers both propagate `peerDependencies` (`npm.ts:49`, `pnpm.ts:71`); berry is the odd one out. Compare `test/parsers/yarn-berry.test.ts`, which has a case named "parses package with engines field without error" — it asserts the parse does not throw, never that engines survive.

## Impact

On a Yarn Berry project the peer analysis — half the tool's stated purpose — depends entirely on the registry pass succeeding for every package. Under `--offline`, or on any registry miss (see the registry-failure finding), berry users get no peer constraints at all and a silently over-permissive range.

## Fix

Widen the parse type and propagate both fields:

    const parsed = parseSyml(content) as Record<string, {
      version?: string
      dependencies?: Record<string, string>
      peerDependencies?: Record<string, string>
    }>
    ...
    result.push({ name, version, peerDependencies: entry.peerDependencies })

Yarn Berry lockfiles do not record `engines`, so leave that to the registry pass. Extend the berry test to assert `peerDependencies` round-trips.

## Resolution
Introduced a YarnBerryEntry interface (version/dependencies/peerDependencies) replacing the too-narrow Record<string, Record<string,string>> cast, and parseYarnBerryLockfile now propagates entry.peerDependencies. Engines are still left to the registry pass - berry lockfiles do not record them. Test asserts react-dom's peerDependencies round-trip.
title: Yarn Berry parser discards peerDependencies present in the lockfile
Zero coverage on subsumption and OR-ranges — the module's two bug sites

body:
## Problem

`setVersionData` (`cache/index.ts:78`) and `setLatestData` (`cache/index.ts:111`) each call `save()` immediately after `setKey()`. `flat-cache.save()` serializes the _entire_ store and rewrites the file.

## Impact

A cold run over N packages performs up to 2N writes, and write k serializes k accumulated entries — O(N²) bytes written. For the 214-package example in the README that is ~428 rewrites of a growing JSON file; for a 2000-package monorepo lockfile it is ~4000 rewrites of a file that ends in the megabytes. The work is fsync-bound and lands on the user's real cache directory, so it also multiplies disk wear on every invocation. It is pure overhead: nothing reads the cache file mid-run, only the in-memory store.

## Evidence

`cache/index.ts:76-79` and `cache/index.ts:104-112` — `save()` is unconditional and inside the per-key setter. The only readers, `getVersionData`/`getLatestData`, go through `getKey()` against the in-memory store, never the file.

## Fix

Drop `save()` from both setters and flush once at process exit, after the render in `cli.ts`:

    // cache/index.ts
    export function flushCache(): void {
      versionsStore?.save()
      latestStore?.save()
    }

    // cli.ts, after console.log(output)
    flushCache()

Also call it from the `main().catch` handler (`cli.ts:187`) before `process.exit(1)` so a partial run still keeps what it fetched.

## Resolution
Removed save() from setVersionData and setLatestData; added flushCache() called once after render in cli.ts and again in the main().catch handler so a failed run still keeps what it fetched. Two tests cover persistence-after-flush and the no-op case.
title: Cache is fully serialized to disk on every single key write

body:
## Problem

`fetch(url)` at `client.ts:57` and `client.ts:90` is called with no `AbortSignal` and no timeout. Node's `fetch` has no default request timeout, so a connection that opens and then stalls — a hung corporate proxy, a black-holed route, a registry under load — leaves the promise pending indefinitely.

## Impact

`resolveRegistry` awaits each batch sequentially (`client.ts:164-170`), so one stalled request blocks the entire run. The ora spinner keeps animating, so the user sees a live-looking process that will never finish and never errors out; the only escape is Ctrl-C, which leaves the terminal cursor hidden (ora hides it on `start()` and only restores on `succeed`/`fail`).

## Evidence

`client.ts:55-68` and `client.ts:88-104` — the `try` blocks catch rejections but nothing ever produces one for a stalled socket. No `signal`, no `AbortSignal.timeout`, no agent-level timeout is configured anywhere in the repo.

## Fix

Node 24 has `AbortSignal.timeout`, and the repo targets `node24` (tsup.config.ts:6):

    const REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS = 10_000
    const res = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS) })

in both `fetchManifest` and `fetchLatest`. The existing `catch` already turns the resulting `TimeoutError` into `null`; combine with the registry-failure warning so timeouts are counted and surfaced rather than silently dropped.

## Resolution
Both fetch calls now pass signal: AbortSignal.timeout(REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS) with a 10s constant. Node 24 is the build target so AbortSignal.timeout is available. Timeouts surface through the existing catch, which now also increments the failure counter, so a stalled registry is both bounded and reported.
title: Registry fetches have no timeout; the CLI can hang forever

body:
## Problem

`computeIntersection` returns `{ intersection: null, conflicts: [] }` in two semantically opposite situations: when there is genuinely nothing to intersect, and when every input range failed `semver.validRange` (`intersect.ts:72-76`). `safeRangeText` cannot tell them apart — it branches only on `rangeCount === 0` (`table.ts:52`), and `rangeCount` is `target.ranges.length` (`table.ts:79`), which counts the _unfiltered_ entries.

## Evidence

Ran the real function:

    computeIntersection([{range:'garbage'}, {range:'also-bad'}])
    -> {"intersection":null,"conflicts":[]}

`target.ranges.length` is 2, so `safeRangeText(null, 2)` falls through to the final branch and renders `⚠  conflict — no safe range` (`table.ts:55`), while the "Conflicts at installed" section (`table.ts:105`) prints nothing because `conflicts` is empty. The user is told there is an irreconcilable conflict and shown zero packages causing it.

## Impact

Non-semver engine values are common in the wild (`"node": "current"`, `"npm": "please-use-yarn"`, git URLs in peer ranges). One such package turns a healthy report into a phantom conflict with no way to identify the culprit, which is worse than useless — it sends the user hunting a nonexistent problem.

## Fix

Distinguish the states in `IntersectionResult`:

    export interface IntersectionResult {
      intersection: string | null
      conflicts: RangeEntry[]
      invalid: RangeEntry[]     // ranges that failed semver.validRange
    }

populate `invalid` from the complement of the `valid` filter at `intersect.ts:72`, and in `safeRangeText` render `— (no parseable constraints)` when `conflicts.length === 0`. List the offending package names in a new section so they are actionable.

## Resolution
IntersectionResult gained an 'invalid' array; AnalysisTarget gained invalidRanges/latestInvalidRanges; safeRangeText now branches on conflictCount then invalidCount and renders '- (no parseable constraints)' instead of a phantom conflict. renderTarget lists the offending packages under 'Unparseable ranges'. Two renderer tests plus two analyzer tests cover it.
title: Unparseable ranges are rendered as a version conflict

body:
## Problem

The README "Example output" block shows a layout the code cannot emit. Every structural element differs from `renderOutput`/`renderTarget` (src/output/table.ts:167, src/output/table.ts:65).

## Evidence

| README shows                                                      | Code emits                                                                                              |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `semver-ranger — package-lock.json (npm) — 214 packages analyzed` | `semver-ranger — analyzing 214 packages` then separate `Lockfile:` / `Targets:` rows (table.ts:182-192) |
| `node  (engines)  ·  6 packages declare a constraint`             | `node (engines)   6 package(s) declare a constraint` — no `·`, and `package(s)` (table.ts:69)           |
| Package table first, then `Safe range`                            | `Safe <name> range (installed):` and `(latest):` first, then the table (table.ts:77-97)                 |
| `Safe range (installed):`                                         | `Safe node range (installed):` — the target name is interpolated (table.ts:72)                          |
| —                                                                 | `Most restrictive (installed):` header above the table (table.ts:91), absent from the README            |

The README also never mentions the `Targets:` line or the second `--all` section, so a reader cannot predict the output they will get.

## Impact

The example is the page's main artifact — it is what a prospective user reads to decide whether the tool does what they need, and what a contributor diffs against when changing the renderer. It documents a format that has never existed in this codebase.

## Fix

Replace the block with real captured output:

    npm run build && node dist/cli.js --offline > /tmp/out.txt

and paste it verbatim. Add a test that renders a fixed `AnalysisTarget[]` through `renderOutput` and snapshot-compares, so the README block and the renderer cannot drift again silently.

## Resolution
Replaced the README example with output captured from the real renderer (generated by calling renderOutput directly on a representative package set), so all five structural mismatches are gone. Also fixed an adjacent inaccuracy found while verifying: README and CLAUDE.md claimed 'Node.js 22+' while package.json engines requires >=24.0.0.
title: README example output does not match what the renderer produces

body:
## Problem

`const REGISTRY = 'https://registry.npmjs.org'` (`client.ts:4`) is the only registry the client will ever contact. Nothing reads `.npmrc`, the `npm_config_registry` environment variable, per-scope registry mappings (`@acme:registry=...`), `_authToken`, or `HTTP(S)_PROXY`. `fetch` is called bare, with no proxy dispatcher.

## Impact

Three common environments degrade silently:

- **Private scopes.** `@acme/internal` is requested from registry.npmjs.org, which returns 404. `client.ts:58` maps that to `null` and the package contributes no constraints.
- **Registry mirrors / Artifactory / Verdaccio.** Organizations that block direct npmjs.org egress get a total resolution failure that renders as a clean table (see the registry-failure finding).
- **Corporate proxies.** Node's `fetch` does not honour `HTTPS_PROXY` without an explicit dispatcher, so every request fails.

In all three the tool exits 0 with an over-permissive range. Ironically, a lockfile-analysis tool that cannot read the lockfile's own registry configuration is most likely to be wrong exactly at the organizations that need it.

## Evidence

`grep -rn 'npmrc\|npm_config\|HTTPS_PROXY\|ProxyAgent\|dispatcher' src/` returns nothing. `client.ts:56` and `client.ts:89` interpolate the constant directly.

## Fix

Resolve the registry per package, honouring scope config:

    function registryFor(name: string): string {
      const scope = name.startsWith('@') ? name.slice(0, name.indexOf('/')) : null
      return process.env[`npm_config_${scope}:registry`]
        ?? process.env.npm_config_registry
        ?? 'https://registry.npmjs.org'
    }

When run via `npm exec`/`npx`, npm already exports the full `.npmrc` as `npm_config_*`, so this covers the common path with no new dependency and no `.npmrc` parser. For proxies, set a `ProxyAgent` dispatcher from `HTTPS_PROXY` when present. Document in the README that private registries need `npm exec semver-ranger` rather than a bare global invocation.

## Resolution
Added registryFor(name), which prefers npm_config_<scope>:registry, then npm_config_registry, then the public registry, and strips trailing slashes. npm exports the resolved .npmrc as npm_config_* under 'npm exec'/'npx', so private scopes and mirrors work with no .npmrc parser and no new dependency. Three tests cover default, override, and scope precedence. HTTPS_PROXY dispatcher support was NOT implemented - see the note in the run summary.
title: Registry URL hardcoded; .npmrc registry, proxy and auth ignored

body:
## Problem

The MegaLinter job checks out PR head with `token: ${{ secrets.PAT || secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` (pr-lint.yml, "Checkout Code") and then runs `npm ci` ("Install dependencies") before any linting. `actions/checkout` defaults to `persist-credentials: true`, writing that token into `.git/config` as an `http.extraheader`. The job grants `contents: write`, `issues: write`, `pull-requests: write`, `security-events: write`.

`npm ci` executes `preinstall`/`install`/`postinstall` scripts from the PR's own `package.json` and lockfile. Both are attacker-controlled on a same-repository branch PR.

## Impact

A contributor with push access but not admin can add a `postinstall` that reads `.git/config` and exfiltrates the PAT — a personal access token whose scope is typically far broader than the repository. The job then goes on to `git-auto-commit-action` with `contents: write`, so the same script can also stage arbitrary content into the branch.

This is not reachable from forks: GitHub withholds secrets from `pull_request` runs originating in a fork, and the workflow additionally guards the commit steps with `head.repo.full_name == github.repository`. The exposure is to the same-repo-branch path, which the guards deliberately allow.

## Evidence

No `--ignore-scripts` anywhere in the workflows. `package.json` already carries an `allowScripts` allowlist (package.json:60-67), showing the project intends lifecycle scripts to be gated — the CI path bypasses that intent.

## Fix

Two independent mitigations, apply both:

    - name: Checkout Code
      uses: actions/checkout@...
      with:
        token: ${{ secrets.PAT || secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        persist-credentials: false
        fetch-depth: 0

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci --ignore-scripts

`git-auto-commit-action` and `create-pull-request` both authenticate via their own `token` input, so `persist-credentials: false` does not break them. Apply `--ignore-scripts` to `ci.yml` and `publish.yml` too — neither needs dependency lifecycle scripts to lint, test, or run tsup.

## Resolution
npm ci --ignore-scripts in all three workflows (pr-lint, ci, publish), which closes the code-execution vector. Verified empirically in a scratch clone that install, build and test all still pass with --ignore-scripts; the four @ivuorinen config postinstalls only scaffold a config file when none exists, and esbuild resolves its binary from the platform optionalDependency. persist-credentials: false was deliberately NOT applied - git-auto-commit-action takes no token input and pushes with the persisted credentials, so it would break the workflow; a comment in pr-lint.yml records why.
title: npm ci runs untrusted lifecycle scripts beside a persisted write-scoped token

body:
## Problem

`.npmrc` contains a single line: `audit-level=critical`. This sets the threshold at which `npm audit` exits non-zero, so High-severity advisories — the bulk of real-world npm CVEs — do not fail the command.

## Evidence

`.npmrc:1` `audit-level=critical`. The npm default is `low`. `grype dir:.` currently reports a High (`GHSA-qwcr-r2fm-qrc7`, body-parser 1.20.1); it is in `test/fixtures/` and correctly suppressed by `.grype.yaml`, but the `.npmrc` setting is global and would equally hide a High in a real production dependency.

## Impact

Latent rather than active — no workflow currently runs `npm audit`, so nothing is being suppressed in CI today. The risk is that adding an audit step later would produce a check that looks like it gates and does not.

## Fix

Either drop the file (the default of `low` is the safe choice for an eight-dependency project), or raise it to `high` and add a comment explaining the exception. If the intent was to avoid transitive dev-dependency noise, scope it instead: `npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high`.

## Resolution
.npmrc raised from audit-level=critical to audit-level=high, with a comment explaining the choice.
title: audit-level=critical suppresses high-severity audit failures

body:
## Problem

The v1 branch of `parseNpmLockfile` returns `{name, version}` only (`npm.ts:57-60`) — correctly, since the v1 format records no `engines` or `peerDependencies`. All constraint data must therefore come from `resolveLocal` or the registry pass. Under `--offline` with no `node_modules` present, neither supplies anything.

## Impact

The run completes, prints `Parsed package-lock.json (N packages)`, and renders a table whose only content is `Targets: none` — indistinguishable from a project that genuinely declares no constraints. Nothing tells the user the combination of inputs they chose cannot produce an answer.

Also at `npm.ts:32`: `lock.lockfileVersion >= 2` is `false` when the field is absent or non-numeric, so a malformed or truncated lockfile silently takes the v1 path and yields `[]` rather than erroring.

## Evidence

`npm.ts:57-60` sets neither field. `client.ts:143-158` (offline branch) only spreads cache hits. `local.ts:35` returns the package untouched when no manifest is found. `test/fixtures/package-lock-v1.json` exercises the parse but no test covers the offline-with-no-node_modules combination.

## Fix

In `cli.ts`, after the analysis step, warn when the target list is empty but packages were parsed:

    if (allTargets.length === 0 && packages.length > 0) {
      console.error('Warning: no engine or peer constraints resolved. ' +
        'npm lockfileVersion 1 carries no metadata — run without --offline, or install node_modules.')
    }

Separately, make the version dispatch explicit and fail loudly on an unrecognised `lockfileVersion` rather than defaulting to the v1 shape.

## Resolution
cli.ts warns on stderr when packages were parsed but no analysis targets resolved, naming lockfileVersion 1 and pointing at --offline / node_modules as the cause. The lockfileVersion dispatch itself was left as-is: making it throw on an unrecognised version is a behaviour change beyond this finding and would need its own decision.
title: npm v1 lockfile plus --offline yields a silently empty analysis

body:
## Problem

`registryFor()` resolves which registry to contact, but nothing configures how to reach it. `fetch` is called bare at `client.ts` in both `fetchManifest` and `fetchLatest`, and Node's `fetch` does not honour `HTTP_PROXY` / `HTTPS_PROXY` without an explicit `ProxyAgent` dispatcher.

This is the residual of `audit-62ad8201`, which was resolved as fixed for the registry-URL and scope-authentication half. Splitting it out rather than leaving it inside a resolved finding, so the store does not report work as complete when part of it was not done.

## Evidence

`grep -rn 'ProxyAgent\|dispatcher\|HTTPS_PROXY' src/` returns nothing. The two `fetch` calls pass only `signal`.

## Impact

On a network that requires an egress proxy, every registry request fails. Behaviour is no longer silent — the failure counter added alongside the parent finding prints `Warning: N registry lookup(s) failed; the reported ranges may be too permissive` — so the run degrades loudly rather than lying. But the tool still cannot resolve anything in that environment, and `--offline` with a populated `node_modules` is the only workaround.

## Fix

Node ships `ProxyAgent` in undici; wire it when a proxy variable is present:

    import { ProxyAgent, setGlobalDispatcher } from 'undici'

    const proxy = process.env.HTTPS_PROXY ?? process.env.https_proxy
    if (typeof proxy === 'string' && proxy !== '') {
      setGlobalDispatcher(new ProxyAgent(proxy))
    }

`undici` is not currently a direct dependency, so this either adds one or waits for a stable global-agent API. Honour `NO_PROXY` before enabling it. Add a test that asserts the dispatcher is set when the variable is present.

## Resolution
Resolved by using Node's own proxy support rather than adding a dependency. Node 24 ships --use-env-proxy / NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY, which routes global fetch through HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY and honours NO_PROXY. Verified experimentally that it cannot be enabled from inside a running process: setting process.env.NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY before the first fetch still resolved directly (ENOTFOUND against a proxy-only host), because Node reads it during bootstrap. Adding undici + EnvHttpProxyAgent was rejected: tsup bundles with noExternal so undici's wasm loader would be inlined into dist/cli.js, which is both large and fragile under esbuild. cli.ts now detects the case Node cannot fix for itself - a proxy variable set with proxy support off - and prints an actionable warning naming NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1, skipped under --offline. README documents it alongside private-registry configuration. Verified across four cases: proxy+off warns, proxy+on silent, no-proxy silent, --offline silent.
title: No proxy support: the registry client ignores HTTPS_PROXY

body:
## Problem

`parseNpmLockfile` chooses its branch with `lock.lockfileVersion >= 2`. When the field is absent, a string, or otherwise non-numeric, the comparison is `false` and parsing silently falls through to the v1 shape, which reads `lock.dependencies` and returns `[]` for anything that is not a v1 lockfile.

This is the residual of `audit-23df4111`. That finding was resolved as fixed for the user-facing half — the CLI now warns when packages parsed but no constraints resolved — while the dispatch itself was explicitly left alone. Filed separately so the store does not carry an admission of unfinished work inside a resolved record.

## Evidence

`src/parsers/npm.ts`: `if (lock.lockfileVersion >= 2)`. A truncated or hand-edited `package-lock.json` with no `lockfileVersion` yields `[]` with no error. The CLI warning added for the parent finding fires only when zero targets resolve, so a malformed lockfile that still produces some registry hits stays invisible.

## Impact

A malformed lockfile is reported as a lockfile with no dependencies rather than as an error. Low severity because the common inputs are well-formed and the empty-analysis warning covers the total-failure case, but the parser should not guess.

## Fix

Dispatch explicitly and fail loudly on anything unrecognised:

    const version = lock.lockfileVersion
    if (typeof version !== 'number') {
      throw new Error('unrecognised package-lock.json: missing lockfileVersion')
    }
    if (version >= 2) { /* v2/v3 */ }
    if (version === 1) { /* v1 */ }
    throw new Error(`unsupported package-lock.json lockfileVersion: ${version}`)

`cli.ts` already surfaces thrown parse errors through the spinner's fail path. Add fixtures for a missing and an unknown `lockfileVersion`.

## Resolution
parseNpmLockfile now validates lockfileVersion instead of inferring it. A missing or non-numeric value threw the file into the v1 branch, which reads 'dependencies' and so returned [] for anything that was not a v1 lockfile - a malformed lockfile reported as one with no dependencies. The dispatch is explicit: non-numeric or non-finite throws 'expected a numeric lockfileVersion', >=2 takes the v2/v3 branch, ===1 the v1 branch, anything else throws naming the version. cli.ts already routes parse errors through the spinner's fail path to the top-level handler. Four tests cover missing, non-numeric, unsupported, and the still-working v1/v3 paths. All committed fixtures already declare the field, so no existing behaviour changed.
title: npm lockfileVersion dispatch does not validate the version
